paragraphs: Sadly, people accept in theory that they can make mistakes, but this fact has little weight when they judge in practice. Everyone knows that he may be wrong. Yet few people think they need to protect themselves against their own mistakes. They rarely admit that an opinion they feel very sure about may be one of those mistakes. Absolute kings, and others who are used to total obedience, usually feel this confidence in their opinions on almost every subject. People in a better position sometimes hear others disagree with them and are sometimes corrected. Even so, they trust completely those opinions which are shared by the people around them. The less a man trusts his own judgment, the more he relies on "the world" in general.

For each person, the world means the part of it that he meets: his party, his religious group, his church or his social class. A man who thinks of his whole country or his own age is almost open-minded in comparison. His faith in this group is not shaken when he learns that other ages, countries and groups have believed the exact opposite. He gives his own world the job of being right against all the others. It never troubles him that pure chance decided which world he trusts. The causes that made him a member of the Church of England in London would have made him a Buddhist or a Confucian in Pekin. Yet it is obvious that ages are no more infallible than individuals. Every age has held many opinions that later ages found false and even absurd. In the same way, future ages will surely reject many opinions which are common today.

Someone may object to this argument in the following way. Forbidding the spread of error, they say, is no different from any other act of public authority. Judgment is given to people so that they can use it. Should they never use it just because they might use it badly? When they forbid what they think is harmful, they do not claim to be free from error. They simply do their duty to act on their honest beliefs. If we never acted on our opinions because they might be wrong, we would neglect all our interests and duties. An objection that applies to all actions cannot be a good objection to one action in particular.

Governments and individuals, these thinkers continue, must form the truest opinions they can, and form them carefully. They must never impose them on others unless they are quite sure. But once they are sure, it is cowardly to hold back. They should not let dangerous ideas spread freely just because people in darker times attacked opinions now believed to be true. Governments have also made mistakes in other areas, such as bad taxes and unjust wars. Should we therefore have no taxes and no wars? People and governments must act as well as they can. There is no absolute certainty, but there is enough certainty for human life. We must assume that our opinion is true to guide our own actions. So, they say, we assume nothing more when we stop bad men from spreading false and harmful opinions.
